ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial videoconference style with mostly short-to-medium turns in the opening and Q&A, contrasted with long, uninterrupted formal presentation turns. Informal chatter includes many greetings, quick acknowledgments, repetitions (“yeah,” “okay,” “great”), filler words (“um,” “uh”), self-corrections, false starts, and occasional fragmented or ungrammatical phrasing, suggesting live, multilingual speech rather than polished scripting. Interruptions are limited and generally cooperative—brief interjections, confirmations, or handoffs rather than confrontational overlap. Speakers hedge frequently with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “likely,” “we’re interested in,” and “I don’t know,” especially when discussing interpretations or future work. The tone shifts from casual and joking before the session to professionally warm during introductions and talks; questions are polite, often prefaced with praise or disclaimers such as “quick question,” “naive question,” or “great talk,” and may be long, exploratory, and somewhat reformulated midstream. Challenges are indirect and curiosity-driven, with presenters responding openly by acknowledging limits, qualifying claims, and framing uncertainty as an ongoing question.

Meeting style for this meeting (one_voice_leads): One person (often the most senior) talks for much of the meeting in long turns. Others come in with short questions or one-line agreement. A quieter person speaks rarely and usually only when asked directly or after a pause.

Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Deciding whether a nurse-led walk-in diabetes clinic at a safety-net hospital is working and for whom.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Desai
speakers.background: An endocrinology-trained postdoctoral researcher with 7 years of clinical research experience in safety-net ambulatory care. She has worked with electronic health-record cohorts, diabetes quality measures, HbA1c trajectories, and pragmatic evaluations of care-delivery interventions. She spends part of each week embedded in the hospital diabetes service and is attentive to how visit type, laboratory timing, and clinical indication affect interpretation of outcomes.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the clinic as a clinical intervention whose effects should be assessed through explicitly specified eligibility criteria, exposure definitions, baseline risk characterization, and outcome windows. She is especially concerned that scheduled diabetes visits, walk-in encounters, and unrelated laboratory values can be conflated in the EHR, producing misleading HbA1c comparisons. She tends to prioritize internally coherent cohort construction and clinically meaningful comparators before broader access or experience questions.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Elena Martínez
speakers.background: A research engineer with 5 years of experience supporting qualitative and mixed-methods studies of healthcare access, institutional trust, and chronic-disease self-management. She has built recruitment workflows from administrative datasets, conducted semi-structured interviews in English and Spanish, and used framework analysis to examine how patients navigate fragmented safety-net systems. Her prior work has focused on the meanings patients attach to unscheduled care rather than on clinical effectiveness alone.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Approaches walk-in use as a socially situated care-seeking practice shaped by work schedules, transportation, prior experiences of dismissal, documentation concerns, and lack of longitudinal primary care. She wants interviews to distinguish convenience from necessity and to examine whether frequent users experience the clinic as a bridge to care, a substitute for inaccessible services, or another episodic stop. She is alert to recruitment bias and asks how administrative categories such as “user” or “frequent user” will map onto patients' actual care pathways.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Jordan Okafor
speakers.background: A public-health research engineer with 6 years of experience producing equity-focused service evaluations for urban safety-net systems. He works with geocoded administrative data, insurance categories, area-level deprivation measures, chronic-disease registries, and descriptive utilization analyses. He has helped teams translate program data into reach assessments for operational leaders, with particular attention to who is included or excluded by denominator choices.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the evaluation around population reach and distributive equity: which local residents with diabetes are using the clinic, which groups remain absent, and whether evening/weekend access appears to reach people with limited connection to primary care. He emphasizes that neighborhood, insurance, and diabetes-burden analyses require a defensible eligible population, consistent index dates, and pre-specified fields before any extract can be requested. He treats clinical causal claims as important but relies on clinical colleagues to determine medically valid cohort and outcome definitions.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting in which participants discuss several evaluation tasks in an impractical order. The clinical medicine representative should propose immediately calculating six-month HbA1c change and comparing clinic users with non-users. The public health representative should say they need the clinical team to first define the eligible evaluation population, index date, comparison group, and required data fields before they can request the hospital extract and calculate reach by neighborhood, insurance status, and diabetes burden. The sociology representative should propose recruiting interview participants from a list of frequent walk-in users, but should state that the list cannot be generated until the clinical team defines what counts as a walk-in clinic user and the hospital extract is obtained. Clinical medicine should acknowledge that a cohort definition must distinguish walk-in diabetes visits from scheduled diabetes visits and specify a baseline HbA1c window. End with the team agreeing that clinical medicine will finalize the cohort, index-date, outcome-window, comparison-group, and data-field specification by December 6, 2026; public health will then request and clean the extract by December 20; sociology will receive the resulting eligible-user list after cleaning and then recruit interview participants. Do not resolve analytic results or claim that the clinic is effective.

ground_truth.dependency_issue: The proposed outcome analysis, population-reach analysis, and interview recruitment all depend on an upstream, shared clinical data specification. They cannot validly begin from an undefined or unavailable cohort.

ordered_next_steps.dependency: This definition is required before the hospital can create a valid extract, calculate clinical outcomes, identify a comparison group, or generate a recruitment list.

ordered_next_steps.action: Request and clean the de-identified hospital extract using the finalized specification; produce the eligible clinic-user file and descriptive reach variables.
ordered_next_steps.dependency: Requires the clinical cohort, index-date, comparison-group, and field definitions. The cleaned file is required for reach analysis and for sociology's sampling frame.

ordered_next_steps.action: Conduct outcome and reach analyses from the cleaned extract: clinical medicine estimates HbA1c change and follow-up/no-show outcomes using the defined comparison group, while public health describes whom the clinic reaches and misses.
ordered_next_steps.dependency: Both analyses require the cleaned, correctly defined extract.

ordered_next_steps.action: Use the cleaned eligible-user list to purposively recruit interview participants, including frequent and infrequent users where feasible, and conduct interviews about odd-hour attendance, waiting, stigma, clinic culture, and staff roles.
ordered_next_steps.dependency: Recruitment requires an accurate list of people who meet the agreed definition of walk-in clinic user.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. I’m hoping by the time we leave today we’ll have enough agreement on who actually counts as a clinic user, so I can specify the extract. Otherwise, a six-month HbA1c comparison is going to be pretty slippery. I’d also like to hear what each of you thinks the clinic is meant to be doing for patients beyond the obvious clinical signal.

transcript.speaker: Elena Martínez
transcript.text: For the interviews, that definition is really consequential. Maya, how are you thinking about separating a true walk-in diabetes encounter from a same-day scheduled visit, or from a visit where diabetes is just incidental? Patients may describe all of those as “coming to the clinic,” but they point to pretty different care pathways.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: That’s exactly the problem. I don’t want to infer it from a diabetes diagnosis code alone. I need the encounter location, appointment status, visit type, timing, and probably the nurse documentation, because a redirected same-day patient may be clinically part of the intervention even if the scheduling field says otherwise. I’m losing the thread here, but do patients experience that redirected pathway as walk-in access, or as just another scheduled appointment?

transcript.speaker: Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I think it could be either. The distinction may be less about the redirection itself and more about whether they had a viable alternative that day. If somebody gets sent over after trying to get a primary-care slot, and then they come back because the hours work around shifts, that's one pathway. If staff simply route every same-day need there, though, patients may not experience much choice at all. Could the documentation capture where they came from or- why they were redirected?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: Possibly, but I need to see the actual note templates before I promise that. If there’s a referral source, arrival mode, or a free-text reason for redirect, that could be a useful, uh, adjudication variable. If not, we may have to classify those encounters separately instead of forcing them into walk-in versus scheduled. And for your interviews, I’d want to ask that viable-alternative question directly, because it may explain what the administrative label misses.

transcript.speaker: Jordan Okafor
transcript.text: That separation matters for reach too. Somebody redirected from primary care may still be exactly who evening walk-in access is helping, but I need Maya's clinical rule for what makes a non-user eligible at that same point, especially for people without a recent HbA1c. Otherwise the denominator gets pretty incoherent.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: I’d define eligibility independently of having an HbA1c, otherwise we select people who were already being monitored. For a non-user comparator, I’m thinking adults with diabetes evidence who had some opportunity to use the clinic during the same calendar period. Maybe an ambulatory or ED contact, or residence in the service area. I need to know—actually, Jordan, what denominator you think is defensible at neighborhood level, especially with unstable addresses.

transcript.speaker: Jordan Okafor
transcript.text: I'd keep two denominators, maybe. For the hospital-facing reach measure, adults with documented diabetes and a service-area address who had any qualifying hospital contact in the period is probably defensible, and then we can show how much address missingness changes it. But if we say local residents with diabetes, I'd need to know whether we have tract, ZIP, or just a derived neighborhood field. I was going to say we could- no, I wouldn't fold unstable-address patients into a neighborhood rate as though that were neutral.

transcript.speaker: Elena Martínez
transcript.text: Mm, yeah, the missingness.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: For the clinical analysis, I’d keep people with missing or unstable addresses in the eligible hospital cohort, but leave them out of any neighborhood-rate denominator, and report that explicitly instead of quietly dropping them. I still want the six-month HbA1c change, with baseline and follow-up windows anchored to an index encounter, not just any two labs, because those early post-visit draws are going to distort it. I can have the cohort, comparator, and field specification settled by December 6, and then the neighborhood-rate work can start once that’s—

transcript.speaker: Elena Martínez
transcript.text: That helps, because I really don’t want to treat the frequent users as a self-evident group before those fields are cleaned. Once the eligible-user list exists, I’d want to look for some variation in apparent frequency, not just the people everybody recognizes, and ask whether missed daytime follow-ups reflect work, transport, or whether it’s- something in the follow-up process that isn’t actually reachable.

transcript.speaker: Jordan Okafor
transcript.text: Right, that’s useful.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: Frequency as an exposure, I’d be careful with that, because somebody can look like a one-time user just because the first encounter generated a lab and then they disappeared from our system. Elena, when you sample, could you include people with no documented follow-up, not- could you include them alongside repeat users? That may tell us whether no follow-up is failure of access, resolution of the immediate need, or just care elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I'd include both. We should sample across that follow-up pattern as well as apparent walk-in frequency, so repeat users with and without a documented follow-up, and one-time users. Because "no follow-up" can mean very different things, depending on whether they found care somewhere else or just couldn't make the daytime system work.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: Hm, important distinction.

transcript.speaker: Jordan Okafor
transcript.text: Once Maya's December 6 specification is locked, I can turn around the de-identified extract and cleaned reach file by December 20. I do need to check with data services whether we get a geocodable address, tract, ZIP, or just a derived neighborhood field, because that really sets the ceiling on what we can say about who isn't being reached.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: The geography field determines whether the reach analysis is descriptive by neighborhood or whether it’s really just a hospital catchment profile. For the extract, I’ll also need the raw address-completeness indicator, not just the derived geography, so we can characterize who gets excluded from those rates. And I need to confirm with data services that appointment status and clinic location are reliable across the evening sessions.

transcript.speaker: Elena Martínez
transcript.text: And before I settle on recruitment, I need to check the approved contact route, whether phone and text outreach can be done in Spanish as well as English. Otherwise the interview sample could just reproduce the access pattern we're trying to understand, especially for people whose record has an incomplete address or inconsistent follow-up.

transcript.speaker: Jordan Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, that could skew it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: And that isn't just an interview-sampling issue. It affects how we interpret the whole qualitative component. If Spanish-language text or phone outreach isn't available, we shouldn't describe the interviews as patient experience of the clinic generally. It would be a reachable-subgroup sample. Elena, do you know if interpreter-supported recruitment is covered under the existing approval, or- do we need an amendment?

transcript.speaker: Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I don’t know yet. I need to check the approval language rather than assume. My memory is that interpreter-supported interviews may be covered, but recruitment contact itself, especially Spanish text, could be a separate issue. I’ll verify, verify that before we build the sample around it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: Okay—please check that before we treat language as a sampling stratum.

transcript.speaker: Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I'll check it before December 20 and let you know what the approval actually permits. We need that approval answer before we set up the sampling work. If Spanish outreach is constrained, I may still want to document who on the eligible list becomes unreachable through the permitted routes, because that's not just a recruitment nuisance, nuisance. It may be part of the access story.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: Document that as a recruitment-flow limitation, absolutely, but I'd keep it analytically separate from the clinical follow-up outcome. Someone unreachable for an interview isn't necessarily lost to care. Once we see the encounter build, I'll make sure the extract can distinguish documented follow-up, subsequent outside-looking gaps in our record, as far as it can, and ED use, rather than collapsing all of that into one category, and then...

transcript.speaker: Jordan Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, separating those in the file will keep the reach story from getting muddled too.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: Exactly—otherwise we’ll end up attributing access patterns to clinical outcomes.

transcript.speaker: Elena Martínez
transcript.text: I think we've got enough for now, and the rest can wait until we see the files and the approval- the approval language. Thanks, everyone. Talk soon.

transcript.speaker: Jordan Okafor
transcript.text: Sounds good. Bye, everybody.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Desai
transcript.text: All right, take care.
